system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2158-09-29 18:19:00 to 2158-10-01 19:29:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, type II diabetes, and chronic heart failure was admitted for a right second toe amputation due to wet gangrene from a nonhealing ulcer. He was admitted directly from vascular surgery clinic, started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, and underwent hemodialysis followed by an uncomplicated amputation. He recovered well in the postoperative period with no complications, was transitioned to oral pain medication and levofloxacin, and was discharged home on postoperative day one. He was instructed to resume all home medications, monitor the surgical site for signs of infection, and follow up in one month for suture removal.

Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Atrophic gastritis, without mention of hemorrhage

Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
Lower Extremity Angioplasty/Stent Discharge Instructions

Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery,

You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any

       Vicodin was prescribed to you for more severe pain. If 
you choose to take Vicodin do not take it in conjunction with

Elevate your leg above the level of your heart with pillows

It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your

Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber,

maintain your strength and assist in wound healing

band aid over the area

1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications

Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.

procedures.long_title: Arteriography of femoral and other lower extremity arteries

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. You’re here because of a nonhealing wound on your right foot after your toe amputation. We need to check the blood flow there with an angiogram. How are you feeling tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay, just a little tired. The foot’s not hurting much, but it’s been slow to heal. Is that why I’m here again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of your diabetes and circulation issues, wounds can take longer to heal. We want to make sure there’s enough blood flow to the area. That’s what the angiogram will show.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is it a surgery? Will I be out long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a minimally invasive procedure. We’ll insert a small catheter in your groin and take images of the arteries in your leg. You’ll be awake but sedated. It usually takes about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I had dialysis today already, right? I saw the team earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had your scheduled hemodialysis this morning. That helps us manage your fluids and potassium before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My potassium’s been tricky before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it closely. Your level was 5.5 this morning, which is acceptable. We’ll check again tomorrow. For now, focus on resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well yesterday. The angiogram showed some blockages in the arteries of your right leg, but nothing we can’t manage. You’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The blood flow is sufficient to support healing. We’ll continue monitoring and optimize your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My foot feels okay, just a little stiff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Keep it elevated when you can, and we’ll get you walking with support later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your lab results. Your potassium went up to 6.5 this morning. That’s a bit high, so we’re sending you for a short dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? What caused that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. It could be from your meds or diet. As a precaution, we’re stopping your lisinopril and increasing your amlodipine. Nephrology recommended it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on lisinopril for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in your case, it can raise potassium. Amlodipine is safer for now. We’ll keep an eye on your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you. How long will dialysis take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two hours, with a low-potassium bath. You should feel fine afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on dialysis. Potassium is back down. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If you keep doing this well, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your leg elevated, avoid standing too long, and watch for swelling or redness. You can walk, but no heavy lifting for a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I saw some changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll stay on amlodipine 5 mg daily instead of 2.5. Metoclopramide is now 5 mg, down from 10. Everything else stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get hydrocodone for pain, but only if needed. Don’t take it with Tylenol—there’s already acetaminophen in it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I remember that from last time. No driving either, I guess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Wait until you’re off the pain meds. And weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll see Dr. Alvarez in vascular surgery next week to check your foot and circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Just to confirm—I take the amlodipine, aspirin, diabetes meds, and the pain pills as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And keep taking omeprazole, sevelamer with meals, and your insulin. All the others too, except lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gently. Let water run over the groin area, pat dry. No soaking. If there’s drainage, cover it with a bandage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Thank you, Doctor. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if you have fever, increased pain, or swelling. Otherwise, see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The discharge papers are ready, and a nurse will go over them with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep protecting your right foot. No barefoot walking, and check it daily for sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I learned that the hard way. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s how we prevent more amputations. You’re doing the right things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Have a safe trip home, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, type II diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and heart failure was admitted for evaluation of a nonhealing foot ulcer following a prior toe amputation. He underwent a right lower extremity angiogram to assess blood flow, which showed arterial blockages but sufficient perfusion for healing. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout the admission. On postoperative day one, he developed hyperkalemia with a potassium rise from 5.5 to 6.5, prompting an urgent two-hour hemodialysis session with a low-potassium bath. His lisinopril was discontinued and amlodipine increased per nephrology guidance. He was discharged home on day two in stable condition with medication adjustments, wound care instructions, and follow-up arranged with vascular surgery.
